extracted.intended_audience: writers, literature students, and general readers interested in narrative technique
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on using the literary technique of foreshadowing: how to plant hints or warnings about future events, where and how to place them, and how foreshadowing differs from related devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of foreshadowing
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreshadowing is a narrative device in which suggestions or warnings about events to come are dropped or planted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use foreshadowing to prepare readers for future events; it is a deliberate planting of clues rather than random coincidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreshadowing often appears at the beginning of a story, and it helps develop or subvert the audience's expectations about upcoming events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce hints early (even in titles or chapter names) to shape expectations; timing can be early or subtle depending on how much anticipation you want to build.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forms of implementation
rubrics_metrics.description: A writer may implement foreshadowing in many different ways such as character dialogues, plot events, and changes in setting. Even the title of a work or a chapter can act as a clue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose among dialogue, events, setting details, or headings as the vehicle for clues. Vary subtlety: explicit predictions vs. oblique sensory details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creating atmosphere and suspense
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreshadowing in fiction creates an atmosphere of suspense in a story so that the readers are interested and want to know more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use hints to build dramatic tension and keep readers asking questions; effective foreshadowing sustains curiosity without giving everything away.

rubrics_metrics.name: Building anticipation and dramatic tension
rubrics_metrics.description: The literary device is generally used to build anticipation in the minds of readers about what might happen next to add dramatic tension to a story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delay payoffs and stage information releases to amplify anticipation; balance between teasing and frustrating the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Making extraordinary events credible
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreshadowing can make extraordinary and bizarre events appear credible, and some events are predicted so that the audience feels that it anticipated them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plant groundwork before improbable plot turns so the audience perceives them as earned rather than arbitrary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of hints (future events, revelations, twists)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hints may be about future events, character revelations, and plot twists to create mood, convey theme, and build suspense, usually to hint at the good events that will likely cross paths with or happen to the main character later on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Align foreshadowing with thematic and emotional beats—use it to foreshadow outcomes, character arcs, or thematic revelations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot pacing and delay
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot can be delayed by situations or events to give the impression that something momentous will occur to build anticipation and emphasize importance to them, which gives the audience a series of questions, particularly after cliffhangers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use delays and cliffhangers strategically to heighten the expectation created by foreshadowing without stalling momentum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-media adaptation
rubrics_metrics.description: The literary device is frequently adapted for use by composers of theatrical music, in the composition of operas, musicals, radio, films, television, gaming, podcasts, and internet scores and underscores, and incidental music for spoken theatrical productions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In non-literary media, foreshadowing can take nonverbal forms (leitmotifs, recurring melodies, visual motifs); adapt techniques to the affordances of the medium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrated emotional investment
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreshadowing can be accomplished by the use of story-driven or fictional events which can bring original dialogue, emotional investment in the plot, such as for the main character, unknown and present characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embed foreshadowing in scenes that deepen character and emotional stakes so that clues feel organic rather than decorative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreshadowing vs. red herring
rubrics_metrics.description: A red herring is a hint designed to mislead the audience. Foreshadowing only hints at a possible outcome within the confinement of a narrative and leads readers in the right direction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether you intend to guide the reader (foreshadowing) or to mislead them (red herring); avoid accidental red herrings when you mean to foreshadow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreshadowing vs. flashforward
rubrics_metrics.description: A flashforward is a scene that takes the narrative forward in time from the current point of the story. Foreshadowing hints at what may happen rather than showing the future directly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use flashforwards when you want to show a future moment; use foreshadowing when you prefer to suggest or prepare the audience without breaking chronology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters explicitly predicting the future
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreshadowing is sometimes employed through characters' explicitly predicting the future.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit predictions can be effective but consider character reliability and dramatic irony; explicitness reduces subtlety, so use intentionally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chekhov's gun principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Chekhov's gun holds that any element introduced in a story—such as a gun on the wall—should later prove necessary or else be removed, emphasizing tight, economical storytelling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that foreshadowed elements pay off later; avoid introducing seemingly important details that never contribute to the plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sideshadowing as contrast
rubrics_metrics.description: Sideshadowing is the practice of including scenes that turn out to have no relevance to the plot, which intends to increase the verisimilitude of the fiction because the audience knows that in real life, unlike in novels, most events are in fact inconsequential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sideshadowing deliberately to create realism or structural ambiguity, but recognize it contrasts with the purposeful signal-and-payoff logic of foreshadowing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation to flashback
rubrics_metrics.description: A flashback is the interruption of a sequential narrative plot to present important events that have happened in the past to present plot points that are difficult to bring into the narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use flashbacks to reveal past events that clarify or retroactively justify foreshadowed elements; do not conflate mechanisms—flashbacks reveal past facts, foreshadowing signals future developments.
